bib.title: Winning Gold at IMO 2025 with a Model-Agnostic Verification-and-Refinement Pipeline

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Winning Gold at IMO 2025 with a Model-Agnostic Verification-and-Refinement Pipeline" (arXiv 2507.15855v4, cs.AI, 30 Sep 2025; first posted as "Gemini 2.5 Pro Capable of Winning Gold at IMO 2025"). Yichen Huang and Lin F. Yang (UCLA). Preprint, no venue stated. Code: https://github.com/lyang36/IMO25

COVERAGE: I read the main text in full: characters 0-36,669, which end at the references. I skimmed the references (to 41,500). The appendix runs from about 41,500 to the end, 176,937 chars total. It is verbatim model-written proofs, which I sampled and did not read in full. Appendix A has the hint-free proofs from all three models and Appendix B has the early hint-based proofs. Scratch text is in /tmp/papers-t3/loop-2/imo/t.txt.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: A solver, verifier and correction loop solved 5 of 6 IMO 2025 problems with each of three base models (Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-4, GPT-5).
  number: 5/6 (about 85.7%) for each model
  setup: Natural-language proofs, not Lean. One base LLM acts as both solver and verifier. Temperature 0.1 for Gemini and Grok, maximum thinking budget (32,768 tokens) for Gemini, high reasoning effort for GPT-5. Web search, code and all other tools disabled. Proofs were checked against the official problems, and the full proofs are in Appendix A.
  quote: "Equipped with any of the three leading models—Gemini 2.5 Pro, Grok-4, or GPT-5—our pipeline correctly solved 5 out of the 6 problems (≈85.7% accuracy)."
  where: Abstract; Sec 4.1 (about char 29,000)
- Claim: The baseline is far lower. MathArena used best-of-32 with self-selection and a human grader.
  number: 31.6% (Gemini), 21.4% (Grok-4), 38.1% (GPT-5)
  setup: A baseline from MathArena [3], which the authors did not run. For each problem, 32 solutions were generated and the model chose the most promising one for human grading.
  quote: "Even with this performance-boosting inference-time method, the reported accuracies were only 31.6% for Gemini 2.5 Pro, 21.4% for Grok-4, and 38.1% for GPT-5."
  where: Sec 1 (about char 5,000)
- Claim: The pipeline has six steps. After an initial solve and a self-improvement pass, it alternates verify, optional bug-report review and correct.
  number: acceptance requires 5 verifier passes; the figure shows a reject rule after 10 steps
  setup: Steps are: 1 initial solution, 2 self-improvement, 3 verify and write a bug report, 4 review the bug report (optional), 5 correct and return to 3, 6 accept or reject. The whole procedure is repeated, in parallel or in serial, to get one correct solution. Accept is "robustly passes". Reject is "always critical errors or major justification gaps".
  quote: "At the time we plan to accept a solution, we do not wish the verifier to miss any issue; we run the verifier five times and accept a solution only if it passes every time."
  where: Sec 2.3 (about char 8,000) and Fig 1 (about char 4,400)
  The extracted Fig 1 labels are garbled: "failed consecutively passes 5 timesw/ major issue for 10 steps". My reading is "reject after 10 consecutive iterations with a major issue; accept after 5 consecutive passes". The text does not state the reject count outside the figure, so confirm from the figure.
  The paper gives no total iteration counts, no token cost, no per-problem attempt counts and no wall-clock time.
- Claim: Step 2 (self-improvement) exists because one query's reasoning budget is too small.
  number: 32,768 thinking tokens (the Gemini 2.5 Pro maximum)
  setup: Gemini 2.5 Pro in Step 1.
  quote: "The maximum number of thinking tokens for Gemini 2.5 Pro is 32,768, which is not enough for solving a typical IMO problem. We observe that in Step 1, the model almost always uses up this budget."
  where: Sec 2.2
  They also write "Step 2 effectively injects another budget of reasoning tokens". Initial Step 1 solutions were of low quality.
- Claim: The verifier is a separate prompt that must only find issues. It sorts them into critical errors and justification gaps, and it must not fix anything.
  number: none
  setup: The verifier produces a Summary plus a step-by-step Detailed Verification Log. After a critical error it skips dependent steps but still checks independent branches (for example other cases). After a justification gap it assumes the step's conclusion and continues.
  quote: "Your sole task is to find and report all issues in the provided solution. You must act as a verifier, NOT a solver. Do NOT attempt to correct the errors or fill the gaps you find."
  where: Sec 3.2 (the prompt is reproduced there)
- Claim: The solver prompt favors honesty over guessing. If no full solution exists, it must give only rigorously proven partial results.
  number: none
  quote: "If you cannot find a complete solution, you must not guess or create a solution that appears correct but contains hidden flaws or justification gaps."
  where: Sec 3.1
- Claim: Verifier quality is qualitative only. The authors rely on repeated runs, a bug-report review step and solver pushback to absorb verifier mistakes.
  number: none (the authors say they have no quantitative verifier results)
  quote: "Since our major goal is not to benchmark the verifier, we do not have quantitative results on its effectiveness."
  where: Sec 2.3
  Further quotes: "Critical errors are seldom missed by the verifier." And: "we instruct the model (who generates the solution) to review each item in the bug report. If the model does not agree with a particular item, it is encouraged to revise its solution".
- Claim: Third-party replication on IMC 2025 (undergraduate competition) with Gemini 2.5 Pro as the "Gemini agent".
  number: 94.5% (rank #3 of 434 humans) against 57.7% (rank #92) for the base model
  setup: MathArena ran the authors' public code. IMC 2025 took place after the code release, so it is uncontaminated.
  quote: "The Gemini agent achieved an accuracy of 94.5%, a score that would have placed it at rank #3 among the 434 human participants in the official competition [1]. By contrast, the base Gemini 2.5 Pro model scored only 57.7%, corresponding to rank #92."
  where: Sec 4.2 (about char 31,000)
- Claim: Hints (induction for P1, analytic geometry for P2) cut compute but did not change what the pipeline could solve.
  number: none
  setup: Gemini 2.5 Pro. The hint-free runs only removed the hints from the prompt, with no code change, and cost more.
  quote: "This success confirms that the hints primarily improve efficiency rather than enabling a fundamentally new capability."
  where: Sec 4.1
- Claim: Problem 6 failed for all three models. The Gemini attempt found the trivial upper bound of 4048 but its lower-bound proof rested on a false claim.
  number: 4048
  setup: The claim that every tile lies wholly in the left or the right region is wrong. The verifier loop did not rescue this.
  quote: "The consistent failure on this problem suggests that certain types of complex combinatorial reasoning remain a significant hurdle for current models, even within a verification-and-refinement framework."
  where: Sec 4.1, Appendix A.6

LIMITS
- The verifier is not benchmarked. Verifier and solver are the same model (single-model paradigm), so errors could correlate.
- No cost, iteration or success-rate-per-run figures are given. The results are from one set of 6 problems, so the sample is tiny. The 85.7% is 5 of 6.
- GPT-5 was released after the contest, so contamination is possible. The authors argue the best-of-32 comparison is still fair.
- The baseline comes from another group's setup, so it is not matched on compute.
- The authors' own outlook lists untried work. Deep Think, Grok-4 Heavy and GPT-5 Pro were not used because they have no API and cannot disable web search. A multi-model collaborative framework is only proposed.
- The text gives no reject-iteration count outside Fig 1.
- Dated: the gold-medal claims by OpenAI [32], DeepMind Deep Think [23] and ByteDance Seed-Prover [10] are cited as announcements only.
- The paper says Problems 1 and 2 were first solved with hints (v1 and v2), and hint-free in v3 and v4.

BUILDS ON: Kim, Baldi and McAleer 2023 (Language models can solve computer tasks); Madaan et al. 2023 (Self-Refine); Paul et al. 2024 (REFINER); Weng et al. 2023 (self-verification); Wang et al. 2024 (Math-Shepherd); First et al. 2023 (Baldur, proof repair); Kamoi et al. 2024 (critical survey of self-correction; the paper says its verifier design addresses the feedback-quality bottleneck); Du et al. 2024 (multiagent debate, for the proposed extension); Wei et al. 2022 (chain-of-thought). Contrast cases: AlphaProof and AlphaGeometry 2 (formal Lean). Baselines: MathArena (Balunovic et al. 2025).

CODE: There is no code in the paper; the repo is linked above. The load-bearing artifacts are the prompts in Sec 3.1 (solver, with its "Self-Correction Instruction" block) and Sec 3.2 (verifier).

FIGURES: Fig 1 (p.5): flow diagram of the pipeline, covering Steps 1-6, the accept branch after 5 consecutive passes, and the reject branch after 10 steps with a major issue. It is the fastest way to see the loop shape and the stop rules. I did not run figures.py; the caption was read from the extraction.

PROBLEMS: Prompt text extracted with odd spacing and hyphenation, for example "c orr ect nes s". The Fig 1 labels are garbled, as noted above. I found no embedded instructions. The appendix is about 135k chars of proofs that I did not read line by line.
